html:
Antigone is a tragedy by Sophocles, first staged in Athens in about 442 or 441 BCE. It is one of his three plays about the royal family of Thebes, with Oedipus Rex and Oedipus at Colonus.

After a civil war, both sons of Oedipus are dead. The new king, Creon, orders that one of them, Polynices, be left unburied as a traitor. His sister Antigone buries him anyway, saying the laws of the gods come before the orders of a king. Creon sentences her to be shut alive in a tomb. He gives way too late: Antigone hangs herself, and Creon's son and wife kill themselves too.

The play sets family duty and religion against the law of the state, and neither side is simply right. That clash has kept it alive. The philosopher Hegel saw it as the model of tragedy, and modern writers have used it to talk about resistance; Jean Anouilh staged his version in Paris in 1944, under German occupation. An old story says Athens elected Sophocles a general because of this play.
